title: You Try Forcing Unwanted Thoughts Away, Yet Fighting Them Makes Them Bounce Back Stronger
description:
Behavioral & Circuit Analysis — Daniel Wegner (1987): 'Don't Think of a White Bear' & Ironic Rebound Process Theory, grounded in Daniel M. Wegner, David J. Schneider, Samuel R. Carter, Teri L. White (1987) (Journal of Personality and Social Psychology). Empirical findings show that inspired by Leo Tolstoy's 1863 boyhood memory of standing in a corner failing to 'not think of a white bear,' Daniel Wegner and colleagues brought the dare into a laboratory booth at Trinity University in 1987.

At the circuit level, this episode examines how anterior cingulate cortex, dorsolateral prefrontal cortex coordinate behavioral and neural responses, alongside evidence that 34 undergraduates sat alone for two 5-minute periods speaking their stream of consciousness aloud while ringing a desk tap-bell every single time the image or words 'white bear' crossed their mind.

Primary Peer-Reviewed Sources:
- Daniel M. Wegner, David J. Schneider, Samuel R. Carter, Teri L. White (1987). Paradoxical effects of thought suppression. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.53.1.5
- Daniel M. Wegner (1994). Ironic processes of mental control. Psychological Review. https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295x.101.1.34
- Ryan J. Giuliano, Nicole Y.Y. Wicha (2010). Why the white bear is still there: Electrophysiological evidence for ironic semantic activation during thought suppression. Brain Research. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.brainres.2009.12.041

AI Disclosure: Visual reenactments, 3D anatomical models, and narration in this documentary Short were produced with AI synthesis tools from verified peer-reviewed sources.
